summary.en: A shipment of Vietnamese furniture reached Hamburg late and partly damaged. Use the contract, the emails and the inspection evidence to decide who is responsible for what.
summary.vi: Một lô hàng nội thất Việt Nam đến Hamburg trễ hạn và bị hư hỏng một phần. Hãy dùng hợp đồng, email và kết quả giám định để xác định bên nào chịu trách nhiệm về vấn đề gì.

setting: Export department, Mekong Oak Furniture Co., Ltd.
topic: International trade contracts, business emails and dispute analysis

briefing.en: Mekong Oak Furniture, an exporter in Binh Duong, sold 400 acacia dining chairs and 50 tables to Nordhaven Interiors in Hamburg for €55,000. The goods were loaded four days after the contract deadline, and when the container arrived in Germany, 86 chairs were mouldy and cracked. Nordhaven now demands a late-delivery penalty, rejects the entire shipment and wants a full refund, while Mekong Oak's sales manager insists the company is not responsible for anything. As a business analyst intern, you must analyse the contract, the email chain and the shipping and inspection evidence, interview the people involved and write an email to the Export Director explaining who is responsible for the delay and who is responsible for the damage.
briefing.vi: Mekong Oak Furniture, một doanh nghiệp xuất khẩu ở Bình Dương, đã bán 400 ghế ăn và 50 bàn gỗ keo cho Nordhaven Interiors tại Hamburg với giá 55.000 euro. Hàng được xếp lên tàu muộn bốn ngày so với hạn trong hợp đồng, và khi container đến Đức, 86 chiếc ghế bị mốc và nứt. Nordhaven yêu cầu tiền phạt giao hàng chậm, từ chối toàn bộ lô hàng và đòi hoàn tiền đầy đủ, trong khi trưởng phòng kinh doanh của Mekong Oak khẳng định công ty không chịu trách nhiệm gì cả. Với vai trò thực tập sinh phân tích kinh doanh, bạn cần phân tích hợp đồng, chuỗi email, chứng từ vận chuyển và báo cáo giám định, phỏng vấn những người liên quan, rồi viết email gửi Giám đốc Xuất khẩu giải thích bên nào chịu trách nhiệm về việc giao hàng chậm và bên nào chịu trách nhiệm về hàng hư hỏng.

objectives.en: Identify the contract clauses on delivery, packing, penalties, force majeure and claims.
objectives.vi: Xác định các điều khoản hợp đồng về giao hàng, đóng gói, tiền phạt, bất khả kháng và khiếu nại.

objectives.en: Check the dates in the emails, the news report and the shipping record against the contract conditions.
objectives.vi: Đối chiếu các mốc thời gian trong email, bản tin và chứng từ vận chuyển với các điều kiện của hợp đồng.

objectives.en: Interview the sales manager, the buyer and the packing supervisor, and obtain the inspection report.
objectives.vi: Phỏng vấn trưởng phòng kinh doanh, đại diện bên mua và tổ trưởng đóng gói, đồng thời thu thập báo cáo giám định.

objectives.en: Write a professional email to the Export Director with a balanced, evidence-based recommendation.
objectives.vi: Viết email chuyên nghiệp gửi Giám đốc Xuất khẩu với khuyến nghị cân bằng, dựa trên bằng chứng.

documents.title: Purchase Contract No. NH-MO-2027-014 (extract)

meta.Parties: Mekong Oak Furniture Co., Ltd. (Seller) – Nordhaven Interiors GmbH (Buyer)

documents.body:
PURCHASE CONTRACT No. NH-MO-2027-014

This contract is made on 10 February 2027 between Mekong Oak Furniture Co., Ltd., Binh Duong, Vietnam (the Seller) and Nordhaven Interiors GmbH, Hamburg, Germany (the Buyer).

Clause 2 – Goods and price
400 Lund acacia dining chairs at €85 each (€34,000) and 50 Lund acacia dining tables at €420 each (€21,000). Total contract value: €55,000.

Clause 4 – Delivery
The Seller shall load the goods on board the vessel booked by the Buyer's forwarder at Cat Lai Port, Ho Chi Minh City, no later than 15 May 2027. Risk passes from the Seller to the Buyer when the goods are loaded on board the vessel.

Clause 6 – Packing
Each chair shall be wrapped in foam and packed individually in double-wall (5-ply) export cartons. Each table shall be packed in a 5-ply carton with corner protectors. The Seller shall place at least 20 moisture-absorber packs inside each container before it is sealed.

Clause 7 – Late delivery
If the goods are loaded after the date in Clause 4, the Seller shall pay a penalty of 0.5% of the total contract value for each day of delay, up to a maximum of 5%.

Clause 9 – Force majeure
Neither Party is liable for a delay caused by events beyond its reasonable control, including typhoons, floods and the closure of ports by government authorities. The affected Party must notify the other Party in writing within three (3) working days of the start of the event and provide official evidence. In that case, the delivery date is extended by the length of the event, and no penalty under Clause 7 is payable.

Clause 10 – Damage and claims
The Seller is responsible for any loss or damage caused by packing that does not meet Clause 6, even if the damage appears after the risk has passed to the Buyer. The Buyer must send any claim within 30 days of arrival, together with a report from an independent inspection company. The Buyer may reject only the goods that are damaged; undamaged goods must be accepted and paid for.

Clause 11 – Payment
30% deposit within 7 days of signing; the remaining 70% within 15 days of receiving a copy of the bill of lading.

Clause 12 – Disputes
Any dispute that cannot be settled by negotiation shall be referred to the Asia-Pacific Trade Arbitration Centre in Singapore. This contract is written in English.

Signed: Tran Duc Minh, Export Sales Manager, for the Seller · Katrin Bauer, Purchasing Manager, for the Buyer

documents.title: Email chain: Contract NH-MO-2027-014 – delay and damage

meta.Between: Tran Duc Minh (Mekong Oak) and Katrin Bauer (Nordhaven)

documents.body:
14 May 2027, 10:32 – Tran Duc Minh to Katrin Bauer – Subject: Force majeure notice under Clause 9

Dear Ms. Bauer,
As required by Clause 9, we are giving you formal written notice that Cat Lai Port was closed by the Port Authority from 06:00 on 13 May 2027 because of Tropical Storm Kirra. Your goods are ready, but no vessel can be loaded until the port reopens. Please find the Port Authority's closure order attached. We will load the container on the first available vessel.
Best regards, Minh

20 May 2027, 09:15 – Katrin Bauer to Tran Duc Minh – Subject: RE: Force majeure notice under Clause 9

Dear Mr. Minh,
We were only informed about this delay today, which is very disappointing. The contract clearly says that the goods must be loaded by 15 May. Under Clause 7 we will deduct a 2% late-delivery penalty (€1,100) from the final payment.
Kind regards, Katrin Bauer

20 May 2027, 14:40 – Tran Duc Minh to Katrin Bauer – Subject: RE: Force majeure notice under Clause 9

Dear Ms. Bauer,
With respect, our notice was sent to you on 14 May, one working day after the port closed, so the conditions of Clause 9 were met. The goods were loaded on 19 May, the day after the port reopened. We therefore do not agree that any penalty is payable.
Best regards, Minh

22 June 2027, 16:05 – Katrin Bauer to Tran Duc Minh – Subject: Damaged goods – formal claim

Dear Mr. Minh,
The container arrived in Hamburg on 16 June. 86 chairs are covered in mould and have cracked joints. We reject the entire shipment and require a full refund in addition to the late-delivery penalty. Our surveyor's report will follow.
Katrin Bauer

23 June 2027, 08:50 – Tran Duc Minh to Katrin Bauer – Subject: RE: Damaged goods – formal claim

Dear Ms. Bauer,
We are sorry to hear this. However, the bill of lading shows that the goods were loaded in perfect condition, and the risk passed to you at loading. The damage must have happened at sea because of rough handling by the shipping line, so Mekong Oak is not responsible.
Minh

documents.title: Cat Lai Port suspends operations as Tropical Storm Kirra approaches
documents.body:
HO CHI MINH CITY – The city's Port Authority has suspended all vessel operations at Cat Lai Port from 06:00 on 13 May until further notice as Tropical Storm Kirra moves towards the southern coast. The order means that no container ships may load or unload, and several sailings have already been cancelled.

The provincial authorities have also ordered more than 2,000 fishing boats to return to shore and have closed several beaches in Vung Tau.

Exporters of furniture, seafood and garments said they expected delays of up to a week. 'We had containers ready to go, but there is nothing we can do until the port opens again,' said one logistics manager.

UPDATE, 18 May 2027: The Port Authority announced that operations at Cat Lai Port resumed at 18:00 today after the storm weakened. In total, the port suspended all vessel operations from 06:00 on 13 May until 18:00 on 18 May. Shipping lines expect a backlog of containers for several days.

documents.title: Independent Cargo Inspection Report No. HCS-27-0618
documents.body:
1. Scope
We inspected container MOKU 482117-3 and all 450 cartons at Nordhaven's warehouse in Hamburg on 18 June 2027.

2. Container condition
The container seal was intact and matched the bill of lading. The container walls, roof and floor showed no holes, dents or signs of water entering from outside. No moisture-absorber packs were found anywhere in the container.

3. Packaging
The chairs were packed in single-wall 3-ply cartons, not the 5-ply cartons required by the contract specification. Many chair cartons were soft and stained by moisture. All 50 tables, packed in 5-ply cartons with corner protectors, arrived in good condition.

4. Damage found
86 of the 400 chairs show mould on the surface and cracked or loose joints. The remaining 314 chairs are in saleable condition. No chair or carton shows crushing, puncture marks or other impact damage.

5. Cause of damage
In our professional opinion, the damage pattern is consistent with condensation inside the cartons rather than impact or rough handling. Without moisture absorbers, humid air inside the container condensed during the long, hot voyage, and the thin 3-ply cartons absorbed the water and passed it to the wood.

6. Estimated loss
Replacement value of the damaged chairs: 86 × €85 = €7,310, plus inspection costs of €650.

questions.prompt: Was Mekong Oak entitled to rely on the force majeure clause for the delay? Refer to the conditions in Clause 9 and to the dates in the other documents. Answer in 2–4 sentences.
keyPoints: A port closure by government authorities is one of the events listed in Clause 9.
The port was closed from 13 May to 18 May, which covers the 15 May loading deadline.
Written notice with official evidence (the closure order) was sent on 14 May, within three working days.
The delivery date is extended by the length of the event, and the goods were loaded on 19 May, so no penalty is payable.
questions.sampleAnswer: Yes. Clause 9 covers the closure of ports by government authorities, and the Port Authority closed Cat Lai from 13 to 18 May, which included the 15 May deadline. Mr. Minh sent written notice with the closure order on 14 May, within three working days, so the deadline was extended and the goods, loaded on 19 May, were not late under the contract.

questions.prompt: Mr. Minh argues that the risk passed to Nordhaven at loading, so Mekong Oak is not responsible for the damage. Evaluate this argument. Answer in 2–4 sentences.
keyPoints: It is true that risk normally passes to the Buyer when the goods are loaded (Clause 4).
However, Clause 10 makes the Seller responsible for damage caused by packing that does not meet Clause 6, even after risk has passed.
The inspection found 3-ply cartons instead of 5-ply and no moisture absorbers, and the damage was caused by condensation, not rough handling.
The tables in 5-ply cartons arrived undamaged, which supports the link between packing and damage.
questions.sampleAnswer: The argument is only partly correct. Risk does pass at loading under Clause 4, but Clause 10 says the Seller is still responsible for damage caused by packing that does not meet Clause 6. The surveyor found 3-ply cartons and no moisture absorbers and linked the damage to condensation, not rough handling, so Mekong Oak is responsible for the damaged chairs.

evidence.excerpt: including typhoons, floods and the closure of ports by government authorities
evidence.label: Force majeure covers port closures by the authorities
evidence.explanation: The signed contract lists port closures by government authorities as force majeure, which is exactly what happened at Cat Lai.

evidence.excerpt: must notify the other Party in writing within three (3) working days of the start of the event and provide official evidence
evidence.label: Force majeure requires written notice within 3 working days
evidence.explanation: The condition that decides whether Mekong Oak can rely on force majeure.

evidence.excerpt: Each chair shall be wrapped in foam and packed individually in double-wall (5-ply) export cartons
evidence.label: Contract requires 5-ply cartons for the chairs
evidence.explanation: The packing standard that the Seller had to meet.

evidence.excerpt: The Seller is responsible for any loss or damage caused by packing that does not meet Clause 6, even if the damage appears after the risk has passed to the Buyer
evidence.label: Seller is liable for packing damage even after risk passes
evidence.explanation: This clause defeats the argument that the passing of risk at loading frees Mekong Oak from all responsibility.

evidence.excerpt: Risk passes from the Seller to the Buyer when the goods are loaded on board the vessel
evidence.label: Risk passes to the Buyer at loading
evidence.explanation: True, but it must be read together with Clause 10, which keeps the Seller responsible for packing damage.

evidence.excerpt: The Buyer may reject only the goods that are damaged; undamaged goods must be accepted and paid for
evidence.label: Buyer may reject only damaged goods
evidence.explanation: Shows that Nordhaven cannot reject the whole shipment; the 314 undamaged chairs and 50 tables must be accepted.

evidence.excerpt: shall be referred to the Asia-Pacific Trade Arbitration Centre in Singapore
evidence.label: Disputes go to arbitration in Singapore
evidence.explanation: Where a dispute would be heard does not help decide who is responsible for the delay or the damage.

evidence.excerpt: 14 May 2027, 10:32 – Tran Duc Minh to Katrin Bauer – Subject: Force majeure notice under Clause 9
evidence.label: Force majeure notice sent on 14 May
evidence.explanation: The email itself proves that written notice was sent one working day after the port closed, with the closure order attached.

evidence.excerpt: We were only informed about this delay today
evidence.label: Buyer says it was only informed on 20 May
evidence.explanation: Ms. Bauer's claim is contradicted by the 14 May email; she simply read it late because she was on leave.

evidence.excerpt: The damage must have happened at sea because of rough handling by the shipping line
evidence.label: Seller claims rough handling at sea caused the damage
evidence.explanation: Mr. Minh's assumption is not supported by any document and is contradicted by the inspection findings.

evidence.excerpt: the port suspended all vessel operations from 06:00 on 13 May until 18:00 on 18 May
evidence.label: Port closed by the authorities from 13 to 18 May
evidence.explanation: Independent news confirms an official port closure covering the 15 May loading deadline.

evidence.excerpt: ordered more than 2,000 fishing boats to return to shore
evidence.label: Fishing boats were ordered back to shore
evidence.explanation: True, but it has nothing to do with the furniture contract.

evidence.excerpt: Shipped on board: 19 May 2027
evidence.label: Goods loaded on 19 May, the day after the port reopened
evidence.explanation: The bill of lading shows that the goods were loaded as soon as possible after the closure, within the extended deadline.

evidence.excerpt: Clean on board – no visible damage to packages at loading
evidence.label: No visible damage to cartons at loading
evidence.explanation: Only shows that the outside of the cartons looked fine; it does not prove that the packing met the contract.

evidence.excerpt: the 400 chairs will be packed in 3-ply single-wall cartons from Thanh Dat Packaging
evidence.label: Mekong Oak switched the chairs to 3-ply cartons
evidence.explanation: Mekong Oak's own memo shows it knowingly used cartons that did not meet Clause 6.

evidence.excerpt: Moisture-absorber packs: NOT ADDED – team short of time after the port reopened
evidence.label: No moisture absorbers were put in the container
evidence.explanation: Breaks the Clause 6 requirement of at least 20 moisture-absorber packs per container.

evidence.excerpt: the captain reported no cargo incidents during the voyage
evidence.label: Shipping line says there were no incidents at sea
evidence.explanation: Second-hand information: the forwarder has not seen the ship's log, so it is not confirmed.

evidence.excerpt: The chairs were packed in single-wall 3-ply cartons, not the 5-ply cartons required by the contract specification
evidence.label: Inspector found 3-ply cartons instead of 5-ply
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation that the packing did not meet Clause 6.

evidence.excerpt: the damage pattern is consistent with condensation inside the cartons rather than impact or rough handling
evidence.label: Damage caused by condensation, not rough handling
evidence.explanation: Links the damage to the packing failure and rules out the rough-handling theory.

evidence.excerpt: All 50 tables, packed in 5-ply cartons with corner protectors, arrived in good condition
evidence.label: Tables in 5-ply cartons arrived undamaged
evidence.explanation: Goods in the same container but packed to the contract standard survived, which supports packing as the cause.

Notice was sent on 14 May, within three working days of the closure.

facts.text: All 400 chairs and 50 tables were finished and passed the factory quality check on 12 May 2027, three days before the loading deadline.
Minh emailed the force majeure notice to Ms. Bauer at 10:32 on 14 May 2027 and attached the Port Authority's closure order, which BlueWave had sent him.

characters.personality: Direct, precise and frustrated; expects suppliers to follow the contract exactly, but is willing to be fair when she is shown clear evidence.

characters.greeting: Hello. Katrin Bauer, Nordhaven Interiors. Frankly, this shipment has caused us serious problems. Please ask your questions.

facts.text: When the container reached Hamburg, Nordhaven asked Hanseatic Cargo Survey to inspect it on 18 June 2027, and Katrin is willing to share the surveyor's report.
Katrin was on annual leave from 13 to 19 May and first read Minh's email of 14 May when she returned to the office on 20 May.
Nordhaven is claiming a 2% late-delivery penalty and wants to send back the whole shipment because some of the chairs were damaged.
Because of the problems, Nordhaven had to postpone the opening of its new Hamburg showroom from 1 June to 15 July.

characters.name: Mr. Le Van Phuc
characters.role: Warehouse and Packing Supervisor, Mekong Oak Furniture
characters.personality: Honest, practical and a little nervous; uses short, direct sentences and does not like to blame other people.
characters.background: Mr. Phuc has managed packing and container loading at Mekong Oak's warehouse for eight years. He wrote the memo about the carton change.
characters.greeting: Hello, I'm Phuc from the warehouse. I'll tell you what I know about the packing.

facts.text: In early May the usual 5-ply cartons ran out, so Phuc's team packed all 400 chairs in thinner 3-ply cartons, while the tables had already been packed in 5-ply cartons.
Phuc's team did not put any moisture-absorber packs in the container because they loaded it in a hurry on the morning of 19 May, just after the port reopened.
Phuc sent the sales team a memo about the carton change on 6 May, but he does not know whether anyone told the buyer about it.

forbiddenPhrases: my manager told me to lie

conclusion.question: Based on the contract and the evidence, which conclusion about responsibility is best supported?

options.text: The delay is covered by force majeure because the port was officially closed and Mekong Oak gave written notice in time, so no penalty applies; but Mekong Oak is responsible for the 86 damaged chairs because their packing did not meet Clause 6.
Mekong Oak is responsible for everything: it must pay the 2% late-delivery penalty and refund the whole shipment, because the goods were loaded late and some arrived damaged.
Mekong Oak is not responsible for anything: the delay was force majeure and the risk passed to Nordhaven at loading, so all of the damage is Nordhaven's problem.
The shipping line caused the damage through rough handling at sea, so Nordhaven must claim from the shipping line and neither company owes the other anything.

unsupportedClaims: The shipping line handled the container roughly (no document shows any impact damage or incident).
Ms. Bauer never received the force majeure notice (it was sent on 14 May; she read it late because she was on leave).
Nordhaven may reject the entire shipment (Clause 10 allows it to reject only the damaged goods).
Mekong Oak deliberately used cheap cartons to save money (the memo says the usual cartons were out of stock).
Mekong Oak must compensate Nordhaven for the postponed showroom opening (the contract contains no such obligation).

writingTask.audience: Ms. Nguyen Thanh Huong, Export Director, Mekong Oak Furniture Co., Ltd.
keyPoints: The delay is covered by force majeure: a port closure by the authorities is a listed event in Clause 9.
Written notice with official evidence was sent on 14 May, within three working days, so the 2% penalty is not payable.
The damage was caused by packing that did not meet Clause 6 (3-ply cartons, no moisture absorbers), as the inspection report shows.
Under Clause 10, Mekong Oak is responsible for packing damage even though risk passed at loading.
Nordhaven may reject only the 86 damaged chairs, not the whole shipment.
Recommends offering replacement or a refund for the damaged chairs and improving packing control / informing buyers of any change.

documents: Read the contract first – especially Clauses 4, 6, 7, 9 and 10.
Put the key dates in order: deadline, port closure, notice, loading, arrival and claim.
The inspection report belongs to the buyer – ask Ms. Bauer about it.
evidence: Highlight the exact clause wording that decides each issue, not only the facts of the story.
Statements in emails are claims by one side; check them against dates, records and the inspection report.
Where disputes are heard and what happened to fishing boats during the storm do not affect responsibility.
interviews: Ask Mr. Minh when the goods were ready and when he sent the notice.
Ask Ms. Bauer whether the goods were inspected and when she read the notice.
Ask Mr. Phuc how the chairs and the container were packed.
analysis: Treat the delay and the damage as two separate questions.
Clause 10 tells you what happens to packing damage after the risk has passed.
Avoid one-sided conclusions: each company is right about one issue and wrong about the other.
report: Start with a clear subject line and state the purpose of your email in the first paragraph.
Use one paragraph for the delay and one for the damage, each with clause numbers and dates.
Recommend a realistic offer to Nordhaven and one change to prevent the problem in future.

answers.q_force_majeure: Yes. Clause 9 covers port closures by government authorities, and Cat Lai was closed from 13 to 18 May, which included the 15 May deadline. Mr. Minh sent written notice with the official closure order on 14 May, within three working days, so the deadline was extended and no penalty is payable.
answers.q_risk_argument: The argument is only partly correct. Risk passes at loading under Clause 4, but Clause 10 keeps the Seller responsible for damage caused by packing that does not meet Clause 6. The surveyor found 3-ply cartons and no moisture absorbers and blamed condensation, not rough handling.

When did you first read the notice about the port closure? Were you on leave?
When were the goods ready, and when did you send the force majeure notice?
Which cartons did your team use for the chairs, and were moisture absorbers added?

conclusion.justification: The port was officially closed from 13 to 18 May, a force majeure event under Clause 9, and notice was sent on 14 May within three working days, so the delay carries no penalty. However, the inspection shows that the chairs were packed in 3-ply cartons instead of the required 5-ply cartons and were damaged by condensation, and Clause 10 makes the Seller responsible for such packing damage even after risk has passed.

sampleSolution.report:
Subject: Nordhaven claim – responsibility for the delay and the damaged chairs

Dear Ms. Huong,

I am writing to summarise my findings on Nordhaven's claim under Contract NH-MO-2027-014 and to recommend a response.

The delay: The goods were loaded on 19 May, four days after the deadline. However, the Port Authority closed Cat Lai Port from 13 to 18 May, and Clause 9 lists port closures by the authorities as force majeure. Mr. Minh sent written notice with the closure order on 14 May, within three working days. Ms. Bauer says she was informed only on 20 May, but she was simply on leave. Therefore, the 2% penalty is not justified.

The damage: Clause 6 requires 5-ply cartons and moisture absorbers, but the inspection report shows that the chairs were packed in 3-ply cartons and that no absorbers were found. The surveyor concluded that condensation, not rough handling, caused the damage. Under Clause 10, we are responsible for packing damage even after the risk has passed. Nevertheless, Nordhaven cannot reject the whole shipment, because only damaged goods may be rejected.

Recommendations: I suggest that we offer to replace or refund the 86 damaged chairs (€7,310) but reject the penalty. In future, we should never change packing materials without the buyer's written approval.

Please let me know if you need any further details.

Best regards,
Business Analyst Intern
